mainTopic: An ox that kills children (תם and מועד, death and injury), and an ox that kills without meaning to: is it killed, and does its owner pay כופר?
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about an ox that kills a child. A קל וחומר tries to prove the ox is liable just as for killing an adult, but it is rejected, so the פסוק ״אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח״ is needed. The ברייתא then asks whether this applies to a שור תם too, not just a שור מועד. Two logical proofs are offered and both are rejected. So the doubled word יִגָּח teaches that the rule covers תם and מועד, and covers goring that kills as well as goring that injures. Then a new משנה rules that an ox that kills by accident, or while aiming at a different target, is פטור. שמואל says it is exempt only from death, but the owner still pays כופר; רב says it is exempt from both. The גמרא defends שמואל: the ox has a known habit of rubbing against walls until they fall, but it does this for its own pleasure, as shown by its rubbing on even after the wall falls.

steps.title: Shouldn't logic alone tell us an ox is liable for killing children?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes a קל וחומר. An ox is killed even when it is a young calf, so it should be liable for killing minors just as for killing adults.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox that kills a person is treated the same whether the ox is small or large. So isn't it logical that it is also liable for killing minors, the same as for killing adults?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is arguing that the פסוק about killing a son or daughter should not be needed, because a קל וחומר already proves it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an ox that kills, the Torah treats a young calf like a grown ox. The argument is that if age does not matter for the ox, it should not matter for the victim either. If logic can prove this, the פסוק looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that harms or kills a person
Small or young ones treated like grown ones
Isn't it logical? This opens a logical proof.
An argument from a lighter case to a stricter case

phrases.english: An ox that kills a person,
where the Torah made small ones like large ones,
phrases.notes: This means a young calf that kills a person is killed just like a grown ox.

phrases.english: is it not logical
that it is liable for killing minors just as for killing adults?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵינוֹ דִּין שֶׁחַיָּיב עַל הַקְּטַנִּים כִּגְדוֹלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the קל וחומר that began earlier in the ברייתא, which compared אדם באדם to שור באדם.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק ״אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח״
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a קל וחומר already shows that killing minors counts, the פסוק adds nothing new.

steps.title: Rejecting the comparison: a person pays four extra payments, an ox's owner does not
steps.stepSummary: The קל וחומר fails. A person who injures is treated more strictly, since he pays four extra payments. So we cannot learn the ox's law from the person's law.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. You can say this about a person who harms a person, because he must pay four extra payments. Can you say the same about an ox, whose owner does not pay those four?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא knocks down the קל וחומר from step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only works if the source case is not stricter for some other reason. אדם באדם is stricter, since the person also pays for pain, medical costs, lost work and embarrassment. Maybe that strictness is why minors count there, so we cannot carry the rule over to an ox.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say this about one case. This opens a rejection that points out a difference.
The four extra injury payments: צַעַר, רִפּוּי, שֶׁבֶת, בֹּשֶׁת
A person who harms another person

steps.confusionAlert: The rejection does not say the ox is exempt for killing minors. It only says logic cannot prove it, which is why the פסוק is needed.

phrases.english: No. If you say this about a person who harms a person,
that is because he is liable for four extra payments.
phrases.notes: These are pain, medical costs, lost work and embarrassment, paid on top of the damage itself.

phrases.english: Will you say the same about an ox,
which is not liable for those four payments?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קל וחומר of step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole קל וחומר from אדם באדם to שור באדם
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The source case, אדם באדם, has an extra strictness (the four payments) that the ox case does not have.

steps.title: So the פסוק is needed: an ox is liable for killing children as for adults
steps.stepSummary: Since logic failed, the פסוק ״אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח״ teaches that killing minors counts just like killing adults.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why the פסוק says, 'Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter': to make the ox liable for minors just as for adults.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא concludes that the פסוק is needed and explains what it teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 1 and 2 showed that logic alone cannot prove the rule. So the words 'son' and 'daughter' in the פסוק are what teach that an ox is liable for killing minors.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches

keyTerms.term: אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח
keyTerms.meaning: Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter

steps.whatToRemember: An ox that kills a minor is treated like one that kills an adult. This comes from the פסוק, not from logic, because a person who injures is treated more strictly than an ox.

phrases.english: Therefore the verse teaches:
"Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter,"
to make it liable for minors just as for adults.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the rejection in step 2 stands, the ברייתא brings the פסוק as the real source.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פסוק is needed to teach that an ox is liable for killing minors just as for killing adults.

steps.title: Does this apply only to a forewarned ox, or also to an innocuous one?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether the son-and-daughter rule covers only a שור מועד or also a שור תם.
steps.simpleTranslation: So far I only know this for forewarned oxen. Where do I learn it for an innocuous ox?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא opens a new question about how far the rule reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the Torah, the 'son or daughter' פסוק comes in the passage about a מועד ox. So it might only apply to a מועד. The ברייתא now looks for a source that a תם ox is also killed for killing a minor.

keyTerms.meaning: I only know it for this case
A forewarned ox, one known to gore
An innocuous ox, one with no record of goring
From where do we know?

phrases.english: But so far I only have this rule for forewarned oxen;
for an innocuous ox, where do we learn it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּמוּעָדִין, בְּתָם מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the rule from step 3 and asks how far it reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that a תם ox is also killed for killing a minor.

steps.title: A proposed logical proof: just as with adults, תם and מועד should be the same
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests a comparison. For killing a man or woman, תם and מועד are treated the same, so the same should be true for killing a son or daughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is logical. The Torah makes the ox liable for killing a man or a woman, and also for killing a son or a daughter. For a man or woman, you do not distinguish between תם and מועד. So for a son or daughter, do not distinguish between them either.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא suggests a logical answer to the question in step 4. The next step adds a second, stronger proof (step 6), and steps 7 and 8 then reject both proofs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing an adult and killing a child are both reasons for the ox to be killed. For adults, a תם ox is stoned just like a מועד ox. The comparison says children should follow the same pattern, so the פסוק would cover a תם ox too.

keyTerms.meaning: It is logical. This opens a reasoning-based proof.
Since
You did not make a distinction
Just as ... so too. This sets up a comparison.

phrases.english: It is logical:
since the Torah made the ox liable for killing a man or a woman,
and made it liable for killing a son or a daughter,
then just as when it made it liable for a man or a woman

phrases.aramaic: לֹא חִלַּקְתָּ בּוֹ בֵּין תָּם לְמוּעָד;
phrases.english: you did not distinguish between an innocuous and a forewarned ox,
so too when it made it liable for a son or a daughter

phrases.aramaic: לֹא תַּחְלוֹק בּוֹ בֵּין תָּם לְמוּעָד.
phrases.english: do not distinguish between an innocuous and a forewarned ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּין הוּא – הוֹאִיל וְחִיֵּיב בְּאִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a logical answer to the question raised in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That a תם ox is also killed for killing a son or daughter
steps.raayaSupportSource: A comparison to killing a man or woman, where תם and מועד are treated alike

steps.title: A second proof: a קל וחומר from adults to children
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a קל וחומר. Adults are in a weaker position in damages law, and still תם and מועד are treated alike when an ox kills them. Children are in a stronger position, so surely תם and מועד should be treated alike for them too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also, here is a קל וחומר. A man and a woman are weaker in damages law, yet you do not distinguish between תם and מועד for them. A boy and a girl are stronger in damages law, so surely you should not distinguish between תם and מועד for them either!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is adding a second, stronger proof that the son-and-daughter rule covers a שור תם too, not just a שור מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adults "lose out" in damages law, because they must pay when they cause damage. Children "come out ahead," because they pay nothing. If even the weaker group (adults) gets equal protection from תם and מועד oxen, the stronger group (children) should certainly get it.

keyTerms.meaning: their position is weakened (they are at a disadvantage)
their position is stronger (they have an advantage)
damages law

phrases.english: And furthermore, a קל וחומר:
If a man and a woman,
whose position is weakened in damages law,
phrases.notes: Adults are "weaker" here because they have to pay when they cause damage.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא חִלַּקְתָּ בּוֹ בֵּין תָּם לְמוּעָד;
phrases.english: for them you did not distinguish between a תם and a מועד;
then a boy and a girl, whose position is stronger in damages law,
phrases.notes: Children are "stronger" because they don't pay when they cause damage.

phrases.english: isn't it logical that you should not distinguish, for them,
between a תם and a מועד?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, stronger logical proof on top of the simple comparison in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That the son-and-daughter rule applies to a שור תם as well as a שור מועד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר: adults, who are weaker in damages law, already get equal treatment for תם and מועד.

steps.title: We cannot be stricter with the lenient case based on the strict case
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rejects the logic. The Torah's son-and-daughter rule was said about a מועד, which is the stricter case. You cannot use a strict case to make the lighter case (תם) stricter too.
steps.simpleTranslation: You could answer: Do we learn a lenient case from a strict case in order to make it stricter? Just because the Torah was strict with the מועד, which is the strict case, should you be strict with the תם, which is the lighter case?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא begins knocking down the proofs that the son-and-daughter rule covers a תם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מועד is the more serious type of ox. A rule said about the serious type cannot automatically be stretched to the lighter type. So the attempt to extend the son-and-daughter rule from מועד to תם does not work by logic alone.

keyTerms.meaning: do we really derive? (a challenge to a line of reasoning)
a lenient case from a strict case
to be stricter

phrases.english: You could say: Do we derive a lenient case from a strict case
in order to be strict with it?
If the Torah was strict with a מועד, which is the strict case,
should you be strict with a תם, which is the lighter case?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַרְתָּ: וְכִי דָּנִין קַל מֵחָמוּר לְהַחְמִיר עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the logical attempt to extend the son-and-daughter rule from מועד to תם.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole idea of extending the rule from מועד to תם through logic.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It uses a strict case (מועד) to make a lighter case (תם) stricter, and that kind of reasoning is not allowed.

steps.title: Adults are different because they are obligated in מצוות
steps.stepSummary: A second rejection. Adults may get more protection because they are obligated in מצוות. Children are exempt from מצוות, so the קל וחומר from adults falls apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also: you said this about a man and a woman, who are obligated in מצוות. Can you say the same about a boy and a girl, who are exempt from מצוות?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second reason to throw out the קל וחומר from adults.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר said children are "stronger" than adults. But in another way adults are more important, since they are obligated in מצוות. So maybe only adults get the strict treatment from a תם, and the proof from adults to children fails.

keyTerms.meaning: obligated to keep the מצוות
exempt from the מצוות
can you say? (can the same apply?)

phrases.english: And furthermore: if you said this about a man and a woman,
that is because they are obligated in מצוות;
can you say it about a boy and a girl,
who are exempt from the מצוות?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד: אִם אָמַרְתָּ בְּאִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה שֶׁכֵּן חַיָּיבִין בְּמִצְוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second rejection, aimed directly at the קל וחומר of step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The קל וחומר from adults to children.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Adults have an extra importance that children lack, since they are obligated in מצוות, so children may not be the "stronger" case after all.

steps.title: The פסוק teaches that תם and מועד, and killing and injury, are all included
steps.stepSummary: Since logic failed, the פסוק ״אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח״ says יִגָּח twice. This teaches that goring by a תם and a מועד are both included, and goring that kills and goring that injures are both included.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the פסוק says: "Whether it gored a son or gored a daughter." This means goring by a תם and goring by a מועד, goring that kills and goring that injures.
steps.whatsHappening: With both logical proofs knocked down, the ברייתא settles the question with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יִגָּח appears twice in the פסוק. The ברייתא reads the extra word as including more cases. So the son-and-daughter rule covers a שור תם as well as a שור מועד, and covers injury as well as death.

keyTerms.meaning: so the פסוק says (the source that settles it)
goring
causing death
causing injury

steps.whatToRemember: An ox that gores a child is treated just like one that gores an adult. This is true whether the ox is a תם or a מועד, and whether the goring kills or only injures. We know it from the doubled יִגָּח in the פסוק, not from logic.
steps.confusionAlert: The two logical proofs were not wrong in their conclusion. They were just too weak to prove it. The final law agrees with them, but it rests on the פסוק.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that when a קל וחומר can be refuted, the ברייתא needs a פסוק to establish the law, even when the conclusion seemed obvious.

phrases.english: Therefore the פסוק says:
"Whether it gored a son or gored a daughter":
phrases.notes: שמות 21:31. Notice יִגָּח is written twice, and each one teaches something.

phrases.english: goring by a תם, goring by a מועד;
goring that kills, goring that injures.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אוֹ בֵן יִגָּח אוֹ בַת יִגָּח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both logical proofs are rejected, the ברייתא answers the question from step 4 with a פסוק.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The son-and-daughter rule applies to both תם and מועד oxen, and to both goring that kills and goring that injures.

steps.title: New משנה: oxen that killed without meaning to
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists four cases where an ox killed a person by accident or by mistake, and rules that the ox is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: An ox was rubbing against a wall and the wall fell on a person; or it meant to kill an animal and killed a person; or meant to kill a non-Jew and killed a Jew; or meant to kill a baby that could not survive and killed a healthy person. In all of these, the ox is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives four cases where an ox caused a death but did not mean to kill this person, and says the ox is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case is pure accident: the ox was just scratching itself on a wall. The other three are 'wrong target' cases: the ox meant to kill something whose killing does not make an ox liable to death, and hit a person instead. The משנה says פטור, but it does not say exactly what the ox is exempt from; that is the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: Rubbing or scratching itself against something
A wall
Babies born too early or too weak to survive
A person who is able to live, a viable person
Exempt

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה just says פטור without saying from what. Do not assume it means the owner pays nothing at all; that is exactly what שמואל and רב argue about next.

phrases.english: MISHNAH
An ox that was rubbing against a wall
and it fell on a person;
phrases.notes: 'It' is the wall. The ox was only scratching itself, and the wall came down.

phrases.english: it intended to kill the animal
and killed the person;
[it intended] to kill a non-Jew, and killed a Jew;
[it intended] to kill non-viable babies, and killed a viable person;
it is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous discussion about בן and בת ended in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox that killed a person by accident or while aiming at a different target is פטור.

steps.title: שמואל and רב argue: exempt from what?
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the ox is exempt from death but the owner still pays כופר; רב says the owner is exempt from both.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: שמואל said: The ox is exempt from death but the owner must pay ransom. And רב said: Exempt from both this and that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the משנה's word פטור means. שמואל and רב disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that kills a person can bring two results: the ox is killed, and the owner pays כופר (ransom). שמואל reads the משנה narrowly: only the death penalty is removed, but the owner still pays. רב reads it broadly: no death penalty and no כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: Death, here meaning the ox being put to death
Ransom money the owner pays when his ox kills a person
From this and from that, meaning from both

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of this section is a challenge to שמואל's view, so it is important to keep straight that he is the one who says the owner still pays כופר.

phrases.english: GEMARA
Shmuel said:
It is exempt from death,
but liable to pay ransom.
And Rav said:
It is exempt from this and from that.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: פָּטוּר מִמִּיתָה, וְחַיָּיב בְּכוֹפֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the word פטור in the משנה from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל: no death for the ox, but the owner pays כופר. רב: no death and no כופר.

steps.title: Challenge to שמואל: this ox is only a first-timer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how שמואל can require כופר, since this ox is a תם and כופר is paid only for a מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why should the owner pay ransom? This ox is a תם!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל. It asks why the owner should pay כופר when the ox has no history of doing this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that כופר is paid only when a מועד ox kills a person. An ox that knocked a wall over while scratching itself has never done this before, so it is a תם. That seems to make שמואל's demand for כופר impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: Why?
An ox with no history of this harmful behavior

phrases.english: And why?
But it is a תם!
phrases.notes: כופר is paid only for a מועד ox, so a first-time event should not bring it.

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that the owner pays כופר in the wall case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כופר requires a מועד ox, but an ox that accidentally knocks over a wall is a תם.

steps.title: Answer: the ox was a מועד for knocking walls onto people
steps.stepSummary: Using an approach רב said elsewhere, the גמרא explains that the ox had a known habit of rubbing against walls and knocking them onto people.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב said about an ox that is a מועד for falling on people in pits, here too it is an ox that is a מועד for rubbing against walls so they fall on people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The ox in the משנה is not a first-timer; it has done this before, so it is a מועד and כופר applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב had already said in another case that an ox can be a מועד for a strange kind of damage, like falling into pits onto people. The גמרא uses the same idea here: an ox can become a מועד for rubbing against walls until they fall on people. Now שמואל's כופר makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with a known history of this harmful behavior
Pits
Here too

phrases.english: As Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: בְּמוּעָד לִיפּוֹל עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם בְּבוֹרוֹת,
phrases.english: [It is talking about] an ox that is a מועד for falling on people in pits,
here too,

phrases.aramaic: בְּמוּעָד לְהִתְחַכֵּךְ עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם בִּכְתָלִים.
phrases.english: [it is talking about] an ox that is a מועד for rubbing against walls onto people.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רַב: בְּמוּעָד לִיפּוֹל עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם בְּבוֹרוֹת
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the משנה is about a מועד ox.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ox in the wall case is a תם, so there should be no כופר.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox had a habit of knocking walls onto people, so it is a מועד and the owner pays כופר.

steps.title: New problem: then the ox should be put to death
steps.stepSummary: If the ox does this regularly, it seems to be doing it on purpose, so it should be killed, which goes against the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the ox should be put to death!
steps.whatsHappening: The answer in step 13 creates a new problem. If the ox keeps knocking walls onto people, it should be liable to death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the ox is exempt from death because it did not mean to kill. But an ox with a regular habit of knocking walls onto people looks like it means to do it. So making the ox a מועד seems to clash with the משנה's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Subject to being killed

phrases.english: If so,
it is subject to being killed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ox is a מועד for knocking walls onto people.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A habit of doing this shows intent, which should make the ox liable to death, against the משנה's ruling of פטור.

steps.title: Why the pit case works but the wall case does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens the question: in רב's pit case the ox may have just been chasing food, but in the wall case there is no such excuse.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense there, in the pit case, because the ox saw some greens and fell in. But here, what can you say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presses its question harder. It shows why רב's pit case had no death-penalty problem, but the wall case does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the pit case, the ox can be a מועד without meaning to kill: it keeps falling in because it reaches for greens growing at the edge. In the wall case there seems to be no such innocent reason, so a habit seems to mean intent. The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, granted
Greens, vegetables
What is there to say?

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל needs the ox to be a מועד so the owner pays כופר, but a מועד ox seems to mean to kill and should be put to death. The pit case had an innocent reason (greens); the wall case seems to have none. The next step gives the answer.

phrases.english: It makes sense there,
because it saw greens and fell in,
but here,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא הָתָם – דַּחֲזָא יְרוֹקָא וּנְפַל, אֶלָּא הָכָא – מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge in step 14 by showing that the comparison to רב's pit case does not hold.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison between the pit case and the wall case made in step 13.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The pit case has an innocent explanation (the ox reaches for greens), so it is a מועד without intent to kill. The wall case has no such explanation, so a habit there implies intent and should bring death.

steps.title: The ox was rubbing the wall for its own pleasure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that, like רב's pit case, the ox here had a selfish reason that had nothing to do with killing: it was scratching itself on the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, the case is where the ox rubbed against the wall for its own pleasure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 15. The ox was not trying to hurt anyone. It was rubbing against the wall because scratching felt good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the wall case has no excuse like chasing food. The answer is that it does have an excuse: the ox enjoys scratching itself. So even if it does this often, its goal is pleasure and not killing, and it is still not killed, just as the משנה says.

keyTerms.meaning: here too, in the same way
rubbing or scratching itself against something
wall
for its own pleasure or benefit

steps.confusionAlert: 'For its pleasure' does not mean the ox enjoyed hurting the person. It means the ox enjoyed the scratching itself, and the person getting hurt was a side effect.

phrases.english: Here too
it is where it rubbed against the wall for its own pleasure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the sharpened question of Step 15 by finding a selfish motive in the wall case too.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the ox's habit comes from wanting to scratch itself, not from wanting to kill.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An ox that keeps knocking walls onto people must mean to kill them, so it should be put to death.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox rubs against walls because it likes the scratching. It has no plan to kill, so it is not put to death, even though the owner pays כופר because the habit is known.

steps.title: How do we know what the ox wanted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what evidence shows that the ox was rubbing for pleasure and not trying to kill.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for proof of the answer it just gave. This line sets up the next step, which gives the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We cannot read an animal's mind, so saying 'it wanted pleasure' needs some outside sign. The גמרא wants a fact we can actually see that tells us why the ox did it.

keyTerms.meaning: from where do we know? (asking for evidence)

phrases.english: And from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for evidence to back up the answer in Step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Some sign we can see that shows the ox meant to scratch itself and not to kill.

steps.title: It kept rubbing even after the wall fell
steps.stepSummary: The proof is that the ox kept rubbing against the fallen wall, which shows that the scratching was what it wanted all along.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because even after the wall fell, it was still rubbing against it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the proof. After the wall had already fallen on the person, the ox went on rubbing against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ox's goal had been to kill, it would have stopped once the wall fell. Since it kept scratching against the fallen wall, we can see that scratching was its real goal. That is why the ox is not killed.

keyTerms.meaning: after
it fell

steps.whatToRemember: An ox with a habit of rubbing against walls and knocking them onto people is not killed, because it does this for its own pleasure. We know this because it keeps rubbing even after the wall has fallen. According to שמואל, the owner still pays כופר because the habit is known.

phrases.english: Because after it fell
it is still rubbing against it.
phrases.notes: 'It' here is the wall, which is now lying on the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17 with a fact we can see.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ox kept rubbing against the wall after it fell, which shows its goal was the pleasure of scratching and not killing.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The wall-rubbing ox is not killed because it acts for its own pleasure, and the proof is that it keeps rubbing after the wall falls.
